content: Ustekinumab is a medication used to treat specific conditions such as plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn's disease, and ulcerative colitis. It works by targeting and blocking certain natural proteins in the body, specifically interleukin-12 and interleukin-23, which are responsible for causing inflammation in these conditions. While it does not cure these diseases, it helps to reduce their symptoms. Before starting ustekinumab, you should undergo a tuberculosis (TB) skin test to check for latent TB, a type of tuberculosis that may not show symptoms. This medication is administered as an injection under the skin, as directed by your doctor. For psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis, the first two doses are typically given four weeks apart, followed by injections every 12 weeks. For Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, the first dose is usually given intravenously by a healthcare professional, followed by subcutaneous injections every eight weeks. When injecting this medication under the skin, the injection site can be the upper arms, buttocks, thighs, or abdomen. It is important to rotate the injection site each time to minimize the risk of skin injury. Avoid injecting into skin that is irritated, sore, or infected. To reduce bruising, do not rub the injection site after administering the medication. Always clean the injection site with rubbing alcohol before injecting. Do not shake the medication, and inspect it for discoloration or particles before use. If you notice any abnormalities, do not use the product. Common side effects of ustekinumab include bruising, itching, pain, redness, swelling, or hardening of the skin at the injection site. These reactions usually resolve within one to two days. Other possible side effects include headache, back pain, or sinus and throat pain. This medication can suppress your immune system, making it harder for your body to fight infections. As a result, you may be more susceptible to serious infections, such as lung infections, bone or joint infections, skin infections, sinus infections, or bowel and gallbladder infections. It may also make it more difficult to combat existing infections. Notify your doctor immediately if you experience persistent nausea or vomiting, worsening redness, swelling, or tenderness at the injection site after two days, fever, chills, cold or flu symptoms, painful or frequent urination, unusual vaginal discharge, burning, itching, or odor, or severe stomach pain. Ustekinumab may rarely cause a condition called posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES), which can be fatal. Additionally, there is a rare risk of developing cancer, including skin cancer, associated with this medication. Discuss the risks and benefits of treatment with your doctor. Serious allergic reactions to ustekinumab are rare. However, if you experience symptoms such as rash, itching, swelling (especially of the face, tongue, or throat), severe dizziness, or trouble breathing, seek medical attention immediately. This is not a complete list of possible side effects. In the United States, contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. In Canada, consult your doctor for guidance. Before using ustekinumab, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it or if you have any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients, such as natural rubber or latex in the needle cover of the prefilled syringe, which can cause allergic reactions or other problems. Avoid receiving live vaccines, such as the oral polio vaccine or nasal flu vaccine, without your doctor's approval. Stay away from individuals who have recently received these vaccines. Do not receive BCG vaccines for one year after completing ustekinumab treatment. Additionally, avoid contact with individuals who have contagious infections, such as chickenpox, COVID-19, measles, or the flu. During pregnancy, ustekinumab should only be used when clearly necessary. It is unknown if this medication passes into breast milk, so consult your doctor before breastfeeding. Drug interactions may alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use, including prescription and nonprescription drugs and herbal products, and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. If someone overdoses on ustekinumab and exhibits serious symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately. In the United States, you can also contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. Regular medical and laboratory tests, such as skin exams, should be conducted while using this medication. Keep all medical and lab appointments. If you miss a dose, contact your doctor or pharmacist promptly to establish a new dosing schedule. Different brands of ustekinumab may have different storage requirements. Refer to the product package for specific storage instructions or consult your pharmacist. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about ustekinumab. It does not guarantee that the product is safe, effective, or appropriate for you. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this medication and your specific health needs.
